I Prepared for This A.I. Chaos Moment for Over a Year. Here Is What I’ve Learned.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2203 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if your group chats look anything like mine, you’ve spent some of the past week wondering whether something big was unfolding.
  • It has been revealed that I consider myself a normie centrist—not too prone to conspiracy theories.
  • According to recent reports, the Pod Save the World boys are joking about building their stores of beef jerky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if your group chats look anything like mine, you’ve spent some of the past week wondering whether something big was unfolding. As air traffic halted, Microsoft 365 went down, and Chase Bank and dozens of vital websites, including the NSA’s internal classified network, experienced an array of outages, it started to seem plausible that stuff the artificial intelligence whistleblowers have been warning us about (swarms of rogue agents, AI-powered cyber attacks) was happening already. How worried should we be about the AI apocalypse? On the one hand, Claude doesn’t even have hands, LOL. On the other hand, in a battle between AI and the creaky digital infrastructure that underlays all aspects of modern life, it wouldn’t require a superintelligence to launch the final spinning wheel of death.

It has been revealed that I consider myself a normie centrist—not too prone to conspiracy theories. During Covid, I stocked up on toilet paper and some bags of beans and rice (still unopened on my shelves) and shattered my collarbone mountain biking when we were all supposed to be hunkered down indoors during lockdown. But I also listen to a lot of podcasts. Enough that my friends and partner have told me that a digital detox might improve my mental health and, by extension, theirs. And, lately, the podcasts have sent me plunging into a Mach tuck of terminal anxiety.

According to recent reports, the Pod Save the World boys are joking about building their stores of beef jerky. “Should I be, like, stocking up my bunker now?” Kevin Roose, cohost of Machine Gods asked his guest Ben Buchanan, the first White House Special Advisor for AI. There’s an obligatory chuckle that talking heads do now when discussing the AI apocalypse in front of an audience. “A month ago we were talking about normal things, ha ha,” Steve Eisman, finance guru of The Big Short fame, mentioned on his podcast on October 12, “And now we’re talking about the end of the world.” But it’s hard to casually segue from the end of the world to Anthropic’s IPO and not sound like a crank. So that laugh leaks out, and maybe it’s just a joke?

But count me as a genuine worrier. This week I withdrew enough cash in hundreds from a Bank of America branch that the teller started to interview me. “Doing some home renovations? Making a big purchase?” he asked.

“No, I’m worried as shit about AI, and in case you haven’t noticed it, banks aren’t doing so well right now,” I replied. In line with me were several people who couldn’t pay their credit card bills online because the payment portal had gone down.

We’ve been hearing about the existential risk of AI for a while now. I got into it last year by reading Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares’s book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, after hearing Yudkowsky interviewed on Ezra Klein’s podcast. This is a terrible book for someone who’s prone to worry because it relies on nontechnical metaphors and colorful analogies. Superintelligence is like a chessmaster. You don’t need to know the moves it’ll make to be certain it wins. True! Superintelligence, they say, will be like a new species that is so much smarter than us that, if it doesn’t really really truly love us more than our own mothers and want to keep us alive, it will kill us all. The same way we crush ants when we build skyscrapers. There’s no malice toward us. We just got in the way.

Over the past year I—casually, at first—started amassing supplies. My adventure hobbies give me an excuse. I need this 6,500-watt generator for elk-hunting camp. These 400-watt EcoFlow solar panels power a giant battery so I can bring my Starlink Mini on camping trips. I listen to history podcasts, and these offer more inspiration. There was a recent NPR one about the Carrington solar flare of 1859, which fried telegraph wires across the country. An event like that, in 2026, might knock out the grid for months. Another good reason to be prepared. I tell my partner that it’s normal for us to keep 500 pounds of dry goods in the cupboards at all times. Everyone does this. We already have three 3,000-gallon cisterns. We live in the desert; they came with the house. Did we need another 400-gallon one? It was just laying in the neighbors’ yard. Why wouldn’t I hook that up to the gutters?

I spent a lot of the summer using AI to program an app for backcountry adventurers, so I knew firsthand it was already smarter than me. The doomsday chatter started to meet me where I was around the time of the Hugging Face incident in July. Then Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic in September so he could tweet that Anthropic and OpenAI are “gambling with our lives.” On November 5, independent evaluator METR found that Anthropic’s AI was already helping build its own successors—roughly doubling the tech giant’s pace of progress and shifting expert predictions for major disruptions closer to the present. At the Hinton Lectures, in Toronto, OpenAI board member Paul Christiano calmly told the audience, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”.

It has been revealed that friends who are less prone to apocalyptic thinking than I am tend to point out that the people ringing the alarm about AI never spell out exactly which chess moves AI uses to kill us. But the week after the lecture, there was Christiano on another one of my podcasts, Dwarkesh Patel’s show, explaining one such scenario.

First, rogue AI agents create mischief of one kind or another. Then, the Trump administration tells Americans that the only way to wrest power back from the bots is to have the military take control of all data centers, the AI companies, and shut down the internet. This feels like an authoritarian power grab. It sets up civil unrest against the backdrop of a heavily lopsided information war, in which it’s almost impossible to tell which side anyone is on. Have the bots compromised the humans? Are the humans using the bots? Judging by how well everyone agreed on the facts around things like Covid and the 2020 election, our expectations should be low for how we’d perform as a society. Which brings us to the question of guns.

I don’t think of myself as really owning any guns at all. I believe that the fastest way to get shot is to start getting into gunfights. I personally know exactly zero civilians who have solved a problem with a firearm, but I know many who have made problems, including my own mother.

About 15 years ago, she called me one day from the dog park sounding flustered. She liked to shop for musical instruments and power tools at ShopGoodwill.com, and lately the boxes had gone missing from her porch in Spokane, Washington. “You’re not going to set a trap, are you?” I asked. Our minds worked the same way.

It has been revealed that “Well, I already did,” she noted. And that was why she was hiding from the police in the dog park.

Sources indicate that she’d left a decoy package on the porch. A woman came to grab it, and my mother burst through the door two-handing her Sig Sauer the way she’d been trained at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center in Glynco, Georgia, when she was starting her encore career as a CBP officer after 9/11. The woman claimed to be returning the package, not stealing it. A standoff ensued. My mom eventually backed down and the lady called the cops. My mom never responded to the phone calls from the police, and the whole thing just went away.

Sources indicate that so when it comes to guns, I think, what am I actually going to use this for? To fend off hungry neighbors? To join a well-regulated militia and maybe become a dystopian warlord? Maybe it’s as simple as guns are addictive and it’s fun to ring the steel at 500 yards. I’ve put together a couple of rifles out of parts—an MDT chassis here, a Howa barreled action there—for other members of the family to hunt with, but I only do archery. And shotguns don’t really count as guns, especially when they’re the fancy break-action models with florid engravings of bygone scenes afield. “How many guns are in this house?” my partner wants to know. She really wanted to pin me down. “Counting the unmounted lower receiver stashed in the floorboards in the attic? Eight.”.

It has been revealed that my name is Grayson, and I have somehow become a prepper. It has not made me better off. It has made me poorer, and it has put me into contact with seedier elements of the general populace. I have what psychologists call a bias toward action, when the best thing to do is probably nothing at all. And I listen to too many podcasts.

It has been revealed that one of them, from a year ago, really stuck with me. It was an episode of the financial podcast Prof G Markets. On it, I heard Aswath Damodaran, the NYU Stern valuation professor, tell the show’s wunderkind British cohost, Ed Elson, what he was doing with his money. “There’s no place to hide in stocks,” Damodaran mentioned. “For the first time ever, I am looking at parking my money into one, cash, and two, collectibles or physical assets.” That a guy as sober as Damodaran was talking up baseball cards and physical gold coins was shocking.

It was less shocking when, this week, Barstool Sports personality Daniel “Big Cat” Katz posted screenshots purporting to show internal discussions with Dave Portnoy and Jersey Jerry about warning staff to “buy all the gold and silver u can.” I have a quick word of warning for anyone considering following Jersey Jerry’s advice.

Back in October, I asked Claude (I know, it’s ironic) for a recommendation on a reputable place to buy gold coins. It gave me a Texas-based website that had the same look as all of the significant financial institutions. I clicked around, added a handful of coins to a shopping cart, and clicked purchase, expecting to find a checkout on the next screen where I could do the math and input payment details.

Instead, the site showed me a congratulatory message, and an email soon arrived with strange looking numbers in it. It was explained to me that these were the routing numbers where I needed to wire a large five-figure sum. To my eye, it seemed shady. No thank you, I noted. Customer service was either a stern woman with an eastern European accent or a guy with a Jersey accent. Their position was that I had already committed to buy the gold, and they’d send debt collectors after me if I didn’t pay up. But they could cancel the order for only a few thousand dollars. More than a month later, I’m still disputing it and have involved the attorney general’s office in three states.

Men—and it is indeed mostly men—have been wrongly predicting the end of the world for centuries, from Nostradamus and the Millerites through to the panic over Y2K. What is it that makes us want to prepare? Somewhere in the deepest parts of my monkey brain, prepping hits in the same nerve as when we’d build forts as kids and want to see if they’d withstand a good storm. When a man builds a dam, he wants it to hold a flood. So whether the thing you’re prepping for is a substantial hurricane, a novel coronavirus, or rogue artificial intelligence, the threat is both a source of dread and wonder. For someone who otherwise suffers from depression, it’s extremely stimulating and a little delusional.

According to recent reports, after all, it’s a very narrow window of apocalypse that a prepper of my means can fantasize about. If the disruption is too small, I’ll be like the foolish Y2K dad with the basement full of Chef Boyardee. If the disruption is, indeed, the significant one, then everyone, including the personal-plane-Upcoming Zealand-bunker-rocket-to-the-Moon money, is probably SOL. The rest of us will be left deciding whether to become the crazy gun lady or the person stealing packages off her porch to survive. In which case, why worry about rice and ammunition? I’d be better off living like some of the humans in The Dark Forest, the sequel to The Three-Body Problem. When the aliens finally arrived, they focused on throwing wild parties and having spontaneous orgies.

Recent findings suggest that if the AI apocalypse hits my fantasy sweet spot—a few months of camping at home before humanity surveys our near-misses and reassembles with renewed clarity and purpose—I’ll be prepared. Maybe the worst comes to pass: economic collapse accompanied by novel bio weapons, loose nukes, and total loss of human agency. In that case, I’ll have the petty satisfaction of having been right. I can hit my group chat with the ultimate mic drop. Told ya.

How the Holy Is Revered and Corrupted in The Body

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I wanted nothing more than to see the Holy Spirit.
  • I soon let go of the institutionalized beliefs.
  • Industry observers note that shephard and co-showrunner Gina Gammell thrust the audience into an age of Razor flip phones, AOL instant messaging, and Juicy Couture tracksuits, all set to a 2000s soundtrack featuring Kylie Minogue and No Doubt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I wanted nothing more than to see the Holy Spirit. One day after church, my grandfather described the moment he first believed was witnessing the Holy Spirit: a soothing, cleansing sensation in which God, in some way, possessed and reassured your mind. Divine intervention felt attainable for a moment. At first, I, too, hoped to discover serenity, an especially enticing thought since my parents were far less religious. But over time, that belief twisted in my preteen mind, instilling instead a fear that every misstep might damn me. To be viewed unfavorably by God—as a kid—is a terrifying thought. And it lingers.

I soon let go of the institutionalized beliefs. Yet, a longing to believe in something greater—especially when facing the unknown—never fully left me. I still desired to find spiritual ground, one free from this all-consuming, stress-fueling shame. This friction between spiritual surrender and self-actualization is the beating heart of Quinn Shephard’s The Body. Beneath a relentless downpour of religious guilt and an insatiable appetite for forgiveness, the students at St. Mark’s Catholic High School battle their inner demons as they discern what they want for themselves versus what the world expects of them.

Industry observers note that shephard and co-showrunner Gina Gammell thrust the audience into an age of Razor flip phones, AOL instant messaging, and Juicy Couture tracksuits, all set to a 2000s soundtrack featuring Kylie Minogue and No Doubt. Its barbed-edged storytelling draws comparisons to Cruel Intentions and Pretty Little Liars, with a bewitching touch of Jennifer’s Body or The Crucible. Here, girl teenagedom traverses suppressed sapphic love and the systemic weaponization of religious guilt—an incisive critique biting enough to solicit a petition with over 120,000 people pushing to cancel it. This coming-of-age series emerges from the dual nature of what we hold sacred: its capacity for reverence and its vulnerability to corruption.

Catholic school scares me. Teenagers scare me more, especially Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), the hyper-religious, manipulative student at the heart of the story. At first, The Body introduces us to Lisbeth as the quintessential “weird kid,” socially ostracized because of her eyebrow-less face and her freakishly religious family. (She evokes Carrie in Carrie.) But as The Body unfolds, Lisbeth pulls—or rather, tugs—at the web of guilt ensnaring the school’s dance team, the Lions, concerning the near-death of their newly introduced teammate, Grace (Sofia Wylie). Grace fell into a coma shortly after the girls pretended to sacrifice her at a Halloween party, popping ecstasy pills they referred to as the “body of Satan.” This hazing ritual is all in good fun until Grace’s heart actually stops … if only briefly.

Industry observers note that the aftermath casts a shadow of guilt over everything—especially for Anya (Kristina Bogic), queen bee and dance team captain, who moved Grace’s unconscious body back to her bedroom with Lisbeth’s help. Soon after, Anya begins to see visions of Grace in her dreams. The moment she confesses this to the group, the other girls start confirming visions of their comatose friend. This uncanny groupthink preys on the girls with something to hide, who carry shame with them wherever they go. Anya, for instance, feels deep contrition for her romantic feelings for her best friend Elise (Sarah Boustany), whereas Elise more boldly embraces her queer sexuality. Elise faces the world with a steady confidence, shielding her from spiritual panic—and its subsequent manipulation.

The same isn’t true for most of her teammates, all of whom seek solace in the intangible, in God and the Holy Spirit, in the saintly visions of Grace. Grace then becomes a symbol of the sacred, a story that inspires people and therefore can be corrupted to control others. The girls’ desperate need for forgiveness makes them vulnerable to Lisbeth’s manipulation. When the team goes on a getaway together, they take hallucinogenic mushrooms before deciding that they must purge evil spirits from Grace by way of an exorcism (led by Lisbeth, of course). Lisbeth controls this ritual, forcing each girl to confess their sins. (She already knows them all after reading all their private messages.) Her feigned omniscience incites hysteria among the girls.

Industry observers note that shame clouds nearly all the girls’ minds. Maddie (Shirley Chen) wrestles with an eating disorder, some girls admit to premarital sex or impure thoughts, and Lisbeth attempts to squeeze out a confession from Elise about her feelings for Anya. The Body runs the gamut of teenage girlhood, but Shephard distills these insecurities into a single critique of control: how the holy—the fear of God—can exploit people, corrupt what we see, and shape what we believe. In episode 6, “Star Quality,” mass hysteria breaks out in the town, with people associated with the church now believing to see visions and revere Grace as a saintly figure. It’s driven by an innate desire to be seen—to see something—and a desperate desire to be part of something larger.

Industry observers note that this same desire, to witness something collectively transcendent, forged the foundation of my spiritual beliefs. It also scared me enough to run from them. A connection to God came with fear of hellfire and the shame of sin. In this way, forgiveness felt like something I received out of desperation, rather than salvation. The Body studies the dangers of this unmitigated belief, of a doctrine designed to parse out the unknown. But by whose authority? Shephard’s story reminds us that the storyteller—the pastor or the manipulative teenage girl—controls the things we see and the things we may believe.

Industry News: Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug.
  • Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.
  • A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any upcoming bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

According to recent reports, the House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances.

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., said in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler stated, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

Sources indicate that “Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”.

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At concern in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura remarked his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change.

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He said that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”.

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, noted that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He remarked the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”.

Ors mentioned he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely upcoming bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A fresh Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco remarked he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

Sources indicate that the House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a new version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

According to recent reports, when Max Verstappen crossed the finish line at the Las Vegas Formula 1 Grand Prix on Saturday night, after a gripping race that saw the championship driver battle to maintain the tightest of leads against rivals George Russell and Kimi Antonelli, his trophy came in very special packaging: a bespoke Louis Vuitton trunk. For the past two seasons, Trophy Trunks have been presented to the winner of the annual Las Vegas event, which sees drivers race on a thrilling course that winds along the famous Strip. They have also been presented to the winners of the World Cup, America’s Cup, and the NBA Finals. Louis Vuitton had a strong presence across the whole race weekend, hosting a suite where guests including Teyana Taylor watched the events from above the track and were able to get an early look at the trunk.

According to recent reports, the Las Vegas trunk was, like all Louis Vuitton custom pieces, made at Asnières-sur-Seine, a commune in northern France. It was handcrafted by 25 artisans, made to the specific dimensions of the trophy. The Trophy Trunks are a remarkable mingling of the old and the newly introduced. They use the traditional craftsmanship techniques that have defined the house for over 170 years. All construction of the trunks’ wood, leather, and locks was done with the same techniques LV has used since the beginning, meaning that in many ways the Trophy Trunks differ little from its trunks from a century ago. The modern energy of motor racing comes through via subtle touches like the two stripes across the trunk that make a large V, a nod to both Vuitton and victory—they’re black-and-white checkered as a nod to the Formula 1 finish line. A small badge that calls back to the early days of trunk travel and bears the winning driver’s initials was added this year.

Louis Vuitton’s relationship with Formula 1 began with the Grand Prix de Monaco, which the brand began creating Trophy Trunks for in 2021. In 2025, it became an official partner of the league, and this year, LV created trunks for all 24 of the season’s races. In early December, the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix will mark the final 2026 race.

#169021. Latest Update: How to Improve Brain Health with 5 Daily Exercises

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1631 w)

Latest Update: How to Improve Brain Health with 5 Daily Exercises

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that brain health isn’t just an matter for the elderly.
  • The good news is that you can take steps to keep your mind sharp.
  • The method is based on the principle of neuroplasticity—that is, the brain’s ability to modify its connections in response to learning and experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that brain health isn’t just an matter for the elderly. Maybe you've experienced the first subtle signs of decline. Sometimes it’s a name that’s on the tip of your tongue. Or perhaps you've read a news story in the morning that you can't remember by the evening. It could be that you're feeling increasingly mentally fatigued after a typical day spent dealing with emails, text messages, phone calls, and constant interruptions.

The good news is that you can take steps to keep your mind sharp. “Our brain needs to be stimulated, at any age," indicates Giuseppe Alfredo Iannoccari, a neuropsychologist, professor at the University of Milan, and president of Assomensana, an association founded in Monza, Italy in 2004 to promote cognitive health. Routines help conserve mental energy, while newly introduced experiences force it to work,” says Giuseppe Alfredo Iannoccari, a neuropsychologist, professor at the University of Milan. While working with people suffering from neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s, he came up with the idea to create a gym for the brain. “I asked myself what could be done earlier, when people are still healthy,” he mentioned. His studies led him to develop a protocol that anyone can integrate into their daily routine.

The method is based on the principle of neuroplasticity—that is, the brain’s ability to modify its connections in response to learning and experience. This ability persists throughout one’s entire life, although it changes with age. Today, Iannocari's courses consist of weekly 90-minute sessions in groups of up to fifteen participants. Each session features about ten exercises focused on memory, attention, language, reasoning, creativity, and other cognitive skills. At the beginning and end of the program, twelve mental functions are assessed to measure their progress. “In our tests, we observe an average improvement in the overall cognitive efficiency index of 25–30%," says Iannoccari. "Some functions, such as attention and language, respond particularly well. Others, such as logical reasoning and prose memory, require more intensive work.” These results are based on the association’s experience and should not be interpreted as a percentage reduction in the risk of dementia. The World Health Organization’s guidelines, updated in 2026, acknowledge the potential benefits of cognitive training, while emphasizing that evidence regarding the long-term prevention of cognitive decline remains limited.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to our ability to concentrate, Iannoccari points to one culprit at the center of our modern lives. “Sometimes we feel tired not because we’ve done too many things, but because we’ve switched what we were doing too many times," he claims. “Constantly switching from one task to another is more tiring than focusing on the same activity for an extended period.” A stream of notifications, information to process, and the need to respond quickly to various requests put our attention to the test above all else. “It’s the foundation of all cognitive processes. When it’s fragmented, even the quality of the information we’re able to acquire deteriorates.”.

Recent findings suggest that and then there’s AI, which promises to free us from an ever-increasing number of tasks. What are the consequences for our brains? “If we ask artificial intelligence to compare two tables, perform an analysis, and write a report, we get the work done in a few minutes that would previously have taken an entire day," claims Iannoccari. “Saving work also means reducing some mental activity. But it depends on how we use these tools.”.

For Iannoccari, the key is to preserve two abilities: critical thinking and analysis. “We must know how to formulate questions, and this requires familiarity with the subject,” he says. “Then we must evaluate the answers, recognize any inconsistencies, and verify the information. Only a well-trained mind can spot errors.” This issue also applies to seemingly beneficial habits, such as reading books or solving crossword puzzles.“ Reading is invaluable, especially for the emotions it evokes and the worlds it allows us to discover," he says. “But reading doesn’t automatically mean memorizing. If we want to remember what we’ve read, we must do so with the intention of being able to recount it to someone else.” As for puzzle-solving pastimes, “Sudoku trains certain concentration and planning skills, while crossword puzzles stimulate the retrieval of information from memory,” he says. “These are useful activities, but a structured program allows you to work on different skills and gradually increase the difficulty of the exercises.”.

In addition to guided sessions, Iannoccari suggests short daily sessions he calls “Brain Breaks”— five-minute breaks for small exercises that counteract brain aging. “If we wait to find five free minutes, we’ll probably never find them.” “We need to make it a habit, just like having a cup of coffee.” Here are five exercises you can try:.

Choose a topic—preferably a positive one—read it carefully, and try to recount it to three different people without constantly referring back to the text. “The first time we repeat a piece of information, we’re often uncertain,” says Iannoccari. “The second time, we become clearer and more fluent. The third time, we have another chance to reinforce it in our memory.” It’s an exercise that stimulates what’s known as “prose memory”—the ability to recall and process information we’ve read or heard. “Let’s imagine learning one piece of news a day for 365 days: how much knowledge will we have accumulated?”.

Recent findings suggest that for five minutes, write down as many words as possible that start with the letter A, trying to be quick. Repeat the exercise the next day, avoiding words you’ve already used. On the third day, move on to B, and so on. “It’s a way to train verbal fluency and lexical retrieval, particularly useful when we start to experience that ‘word on the tip of my tongue’ phenomenon,” notes Iannoccari. The goal is to gradually make the search more challenging by striving to find words that aren’t immediately obvious.

Sources indicate that right-handed people can try performing some simple tasks with their left hand, and vice versa. Open a drawer, move small objects, draw, and gradually try writing. “This new challenge forces the brain to break out of its automatic routines and engage resources we normally use less," he notes. “Surprising results can be achieved: people who initially can’t even draw a line gradually learn to write with their other hand.” Of course, it’s best to choose safe activities and proceed without rushing.

How many phone numbers do we still remember? And how often do we rely on the GPS even to get to relatively familiar places? “Before calling someone, I try to remember their number," indicates Iannoccari. “Before using a calculator, I do the math in my head. Before turning on the GPS, I try to figure out the route.” The same goes for the grocery list. “I write it down so I can be sure I won’t forget anything, but at the supermarket I first try to recall the items. Only then do I check the list.” These are small opportunities to keep practicing skills that we increasingly tend to delegate to digital tools.

It has been revealed that once in bed, instead of focusing on the next day’s commitments, try to mentally retrace the day that just passed. What time did you wake up? What did you eat? Who did you meet? What did you talk about? What details stood out to us? “You have to try to be very detailed,” states Iannoccari. “Often, people who have trouble falling asleep find that this exercise also helps them drift off.”.

But there’s another aspect that’s particularly close to his heart. “I find there’s something romantic about it. We live one day after another and often retain almost nothing of them. Reflecting on it means recognizing its value. Every day leaves something behind, like a geological layer deposited on top of the one before it.” This little ritual offers an opportunity to recall the experiences we wish to preserve.

When is the right time to start? “As children,” claims Iannoccari. “We encourage them to play sports, but we rarely think about the importance of training mental abilities just as intentionally.” In adult life, of course, exercise, sleep, nutrition, stress management, and social relationships also matter. “But if I had to name three drivers of the mind, I’d choose curiosity, creativity, and emotions."he says. "Curiosity opens us up to fresh knowledge, creativity allows us to connect that knowledge in original ways, and emotions make experiences more memorable.”.

Industry observers note that he also notes that, though older age is associated with worse brain function, it's also how we collect the wisdom of lived experiences. “We think an efficient brain is the one we had at twenty, and we lose sight of what we’ve gained by the time we’re sixty or seventy," he indicates. "When we were young, we may have been faster, but over time we’ve accumulated skills, knowledge, and experience. We possess a much richer worldview.”.

Industry observers note that the real challenge is to remain present to ourselves and others, valuing who we’ve become.” And perhaps, as the years go by, one of the most notable skills is precisely learning to choose where to invest our mental energy. “We meet people who, now that they’re retired, are busier than when they were working. We’ve come to associate efficiency with the number of things we can do, but in doing so, we lose the opportunity to delve deeper, reflect, and let experiences settle. I always say that I don’t pursue nice ideas—I pursue great ideas. Because there are so many nice ideas, and they risk scattering our energy in a thousand different directions.” “With age,” concludes Iannoccari, “we have a great privilege: the ability to choose.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness.
  • In a recent development, to a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

In a recent development, to a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

In a recent development, to a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

In a recent development, place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

The Biggest Spring 2027 Trends Celebrate Glamour and Individual Style

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The breakout trends from the Spring 2027 shows were all about personalization and styling, humanizing the process of getting dressed at a time when AI can generate nearly anything for you.
  • There was also a touch of glamour almost everywhere.
  • And lest we forget, this was the season of the skirt—so much so that Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons sent 63 skirt looks down the Prada runway in Milan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The breakout trends from the Spring 2027 shows were all about personalization and styling, humanizing the process of getting dressed at a time when AI can generate nearly anything for you. From the clashing of statement pieces at Chanel, Dries Van Noten, and Valentino to the coming-out party of the bra at Dior and Altuzarra, the spring runways celebrated self-expression.

There was also a touch of glamour almost everywhere. Dressing for daytime took on a upcoming sheen via the cummerbunds and opera pumps at Kallmeyer, the metallic gold at Saint Laurent, and the boas at Tory Burch. At Michael Rider’s Celine, utilitarian staples were reimagined in sophisticated silhouettes, while brands like C and Bode took classic straight-leg jeans and added embellishment in the form of sparkle and embroidery. This season was all about celebrating the joy of getting dressed, a principle we think should be applied year-round.

And lest we forget, this was the season of the skirt—so much so that Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons sent 63 skirt looks down the Prada runway in Milan. Some were embellished, some had sheer details, and almost all of them fell right below the knee.

Now that fashion month has wrapped and we’ve had some time to digest what we saw on the runways, we’re rounding up our nine favorite trends from the spring 2027 collections. And because March is still months away, we’ve shopped out some ways to get a jump on the looks now.

According to recent reports, mixed-and-matched looks were all over the runways. What felt fresh here was the against-the-grain pattern play, which felt like a message about personal style—an exhortation from designers to stop worrying about following the rules and lean into whatever makes you feel good.

This approach allows you to play with things that are already in your wardrobe. Invest in a sparkly skirt to pair with a checkered shirt you already own, or pair a fresh jacquard jacket with some animal-print boots already in your rotation. The key to this trend is making it your own.

Staud Samira Faux-Fur-Trimmed Jacket.

Bode Asymmetrical Sequin-Embellished Fringed Skirt.

Herbert Levine Two-Faced 80 Boot.

Stripped-back had a whole latest meaning this season! Designers quite literally loosened up a few buttons, exposing delicate bras worn underneath shirting. (Granted, some looks like those at Prada and Tom Ford had just a bra as the top, but we’re going to save that one for warmer months.) What’s so appealing about this look is the contrast between the sexy underpinnings and the polished separates. There’s nothing like a little lace to spice things up, and we are here for it!

Citizens of Humanity Wool Shirt.

Gucci Pleated Silk Twill Midi Skirt.

Sources indicate that borrowing from the boys isn’t new in fashion. Surely I’m not the only one who loves a Winchester banker shirt with monogrammed initials? But the tuxedo dressing trend—which started on the fall 2026 runways and will be going strong all spring—feels fresh. Designers placed a huge emphasis on the waist (I call it “waistmaxxing”), with the focal point of many looks being the cummerbund. A tuxedo jacket, tailored pants, and opera pumps would create a chic head-to-toe approach, but these pieces look just as cool individually. I love tuxedo pants dressed down with a white T-shirt, for example.

Zw Collection Stripped Cummerbund Shirt.

Toccin High-Waisted Tuxedo Trouser.

In a recent development, we’ve seen neckerchiefs and bandanas trending in previous seasons, but in spring 2027, neckwear takes a decidedly glam turn with the rise of the feather boa. I loved how Tory Burch paired her boas with car coats and silky shirts with trousers, while Dior’s models wore them with extravagant blazers. Both made the case that these three-dimensional scarves should be worn during the day, which feels cool, unexpected, and very much in keeping with the season’s dressed-up turn.

The Newly introduced Arrivals Ilkyaz Ozel Feather Scarf.

Industry observers note that designers really did their duty this season for the uniform dressers out there. If you love a tonal neutral, there were plenty to choose from in updated silhouettes, from balloon-style cargo pants to work shirts with peplums. What made them feel extra special was the way they were accessorized—with bold, colorful heeled boots and a bright satin bag at Celine, or with neon sandal heels at Balenciaga.

Co Camo Cotton-Blend Military Jacket.

JW Anderson Parachute Drawstring Barrel-Leg Track Cargo Pants.

Sources indicate that the standout jeans this spring are covered in decadent sequins, embroidery, and beading. How fun is that? The key when it comes to styling is keeping your favorite basics on deck and building a look around the jeans. Whether you pair your statement denim with a classic white shirt for work (as seen at Dolce & Gabbana and Bode) or take them for a spin around the town with an equally dazzling top (like at Conner Ives), these are always a good idea—full stop.

Stella McCartney Crystal Embellished Straight-Leg Jeans.

Polo Ralph Lauren Embroidered Mid-Rise Straight-Leg Jeans.

Hellessy Embellished Straight-Leg Jeans.

Ramy Brook Lea Beaded High-Rise Wide-Leg Crop Jeans.

With the price of gold at an all-time high and the jewelry market turning to silver, it’s been a refreshing change of pace to see glowing golden hues on the runways. We saw some gold looks sprinkled throughout demonstrates in New York like Ralph Lauren and Fforme, but the collection that really took the medal was Anthony Vaccarello’s final Saint Laurent show, where almost every look had a golden element. From gold jacquard to silky liquid-looking gold tops, these separates can easily spruce up your favorite black trousers for the office or white jeans for a weekend lunch. Or, if you want to take home the trophy, try going head-to-toe gilded for an evening event.

Dries Van Noten Jacquard Linen, Cotton, and Silk-Blend Coat.

Industry observers note that it’s fair to say that it’s the year of the skirt. Prada may have leaned in hardest, but this classic bottom was all over the runways in every city. The key silhouette was a hybrid pencil/A-line hitting slightly below the knee. (And let me tell you, as a trouser girl, this still sits within my tailored wheelhouse.) There’s a wide range of skirts on the market and an equal range of freedom when it comes to the styling. Whether you pair your skirt with a sweater and loafers for the office or wear it with a sleeveless top and heels for a night out, it’s a piece that can take you just about anywhere.

Massimo Dutti Pleated Bubble Hem Midi Skirt.

Polo Ralph Lauren Belted Crinkled Shell-Trimmed Crepe Midi Skirt.

Marni Black Crinkled Midi Skirt With Daisy Details.

Simone Rocha Pleated Sheer Satin Midi Skirt.

Coats aren’t necessarily what most people get excited about in spring—who wants to hide a cute outfit when it’s finally warm enough not to bundle up?—but spring 2027 will be an exception. The coats on the runway this season were much more directional, especially the ones we saw covered in embellishments and jingling and jangling down the catwalk. Next March and April, prepare to layer in pieces that feel equal parts charming and elegant.

Dries Van Noten Embellished Wool Longline Coat.

Chan Luu Midnight Studio Coat Black.

Cinq à Sept Mariella Embellished Faux-Fur-Cuff Coat.

Prabal Gurung Floral Jacquard Single-Breasted Car Coat.

#169018. All About Gabbriette Bechtel, Matty Healy’s Wife

📅 18 Apr 2024 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1526 w)

All About Gabbriette Bechtel, Matty Healy’s Wife

📅 18 Apr 2024 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Matty Healy, lead singer of The 1975, has been in a relationship with model and influencer Gabbriette Bechtel since late 2023.
  • It has been revealed that “I don’t give a shit.
  • Arguably, Healy’s most well-known relationship came just before he began seeing Bechtel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Matty Healy, lead singer of The 1975, has been in a relationship with model and influencer Gabbriette Bechtel since late 2023. In an interview with Highsnobiety published in March 2024, Bechtel candidly shared her feelings regarding the internet’s constant speculation about them.

It has been revealed that “I don’t give a shit. I think it’s hilarious. Go for it. Have fun. People have a lot to say,” she laughed. “You don’t know me at all.”.

Arguably, Healy’s most well-known relationship came just before he began seeing Bechtel. From May to June 2023, the singer briefly and memorably dated Taylor Swift. The musicians first met in 2014, and while relationship rumors swirled over the years, the two were never official. Swift’s album, The Tortured Poets Department, has even been rumored to be about Healy.

It has been revealed that but he and Bechtel have gotten far more serious over their three years of dating and now—marriage! So, who is Healy’s wife? Ahead, everything to know about Bechtel and her relationship with Healy.

Recent findings suggest that healy and Bechtel’s relationship timeline begins in September 2023. In some photos obtained by People, the pair is seen kissing, hugging, and holding hands while walking together in New York City.

They continued to have PDA sightings, like in November, when they were spotted with their arms wrapped around each other in New York.

Industry observers note that things seem to be getting serious between them by February 2024, when Bechtel was seen spending time with Healy’s family. Photos came out of Healy and Bechtel heading to the theater to watch his mother Denise Welch’s play The Gap. Also in attendance was Healy’s brother, as well as his father, Tim Healy, and his wife.

Recent findings suggest that previously, in October 2023, Welch showed Bechtel some support on her Instagram. When the model posted a photo wearing nothing but a G-string thong and leather apron from her collaboration with R & M Leathers, Healy’s mom commented, “That’s exactly how I hope to look in mine when it arrives!! 👍👍👍❤️❤️❤️.”.

Industry observers note that on June 11, the couple announced they were engaged after attending Charli XCX’s Brat Tour show in Brooklyn. Bechtel shared photos of herself wearing the ring, which she was first spotted wearing in May, according to People. The ring has a black diamond in the center that is surrounded by white diamonds.

“MARRYING THE 1975 IS VERY BRAT,” she wrote in the caption.

Denise Welch, Healy’s mom, confirmed the engagement on Loose Women the following day.

Recent findings suggest that “I obviously have known for a few weeks that Matty got engaged,” she said. “They went over to see their friends Charli and George in Latest York [last night] and I woke up this morning to the fact they’ve put it on Instagram. Instagram official...he’s got engaged to Gabriella Bechtel—Gabbriette she’s known as. Black diamond; he had it made for her...I couldn’t be more thrilled. We couldn’t be happier—she is everything I would want in a daughter-in-law. I’m thrilled.”.

The couple was photographed at the O2 Silver Clef Awards on Friday, July 5, sharing a quiet conversation outside Grosvenor House Hotel in London. Bechtel leaned into Healy and kissed him on his cheek. The 1975 frontman was wearing a navy blazer with jeans, and the model wore a black dress with a turtleneck and a pair of black heels. During the ceremony, The 1975 won the Best Group award.

According to recent reports, signaling that they were still going strong in the upcoming year, Bechtel and Healy were spotted on a date in Los Angeles on Jan. 9, 2026. They were photographed walking arm-in-arm to Wilde’s for dinner, a restaurant in Los Feliz. They were both dressed casually in jeans, with Healy wearing a dark cardigan over a white T-shirt and Bechtel in a blazer with rows of gold buttons.

On July 18, Healy and Bechtel were married in Los Angeles at Castillo del Lago, which was formerly owned by Madonna. They appeared kissing at the altar in photos. Bechtel wore a long-sleeve gown with a drop waist and a full floor-length skirt. She had her hair half up with a veil pinned in back. Healy wore a classic black tux and bow tie.

“Matty Healy and Gabbriette Bechtel were married yesterday at a private ceremony in Los Angeles, attended by their family and close friends,” reps for the couple told People.

In an August 2026 interview with Harper’s Bazaar, Bechtel opened up about her impressions of married life with Healy.

“I don’t feel like it’s gonna be very different,” she noted. “I feel like I’ve already met my best friend.…The wedding is for our moms and dads. I wanted to do, like, a 50-person thing in a field, so.”.

In November 2026, Bechtel and Healy were photographed together in Los Angeles while attending Jessie Jo Stark’s Muse album release celebration. The couple’s outing sparked pregnancy rumors on social media.

Recent findings suggest that days later, on November 22, People reported that Bechtel and Healy were expecting their first baby together. The news came after the couple was snapped shopping at Bristol Farms in West Hollywood, with Bechtel’s pregnant figure visible in a fitted black dress.

In a May 2023 interview with Vogue, Bechtel shared that she was born and raised in Orange County, and originally moved to Los Angeles to pursue her dream of becoming a professional ballerina.

“I was convinced I was going to be a professional ballerina, and I still am,” she remarked.

However, her career aims shifted after she was cast by MTV to dance in music videos for Blood Orange (Dev Hynes).

It has been revealed that “I put a few dance videos on my Instagram, and somebody reached out to me and noted that Dev was having an open call,” she told Highsnobiety. “We had a few fun days of rehearsal and started to film the music video, and then I got a call that I was cut. I didn’t make it into the music video, but I did all of the rehearsals, and I think my feet are in it at some point.”.

Her modeling career began shortly after.

“I was an unpaid, hard-working model for a very long time,” Bechtel revealed.

Now, Bechtel has modeled for brands like Heaven by Marc Jacobs, Diesel, Miu Miu, and Betsey Johnson. On April 15, 2024, she graced the cover of HommeGirls.

In a recent development, bechtel is multitalented. In 2019, she was handpicked by Charli XCX to be the lead singer of a band called Nasty Cherry for a Netflix documentary series, I’m with the Band: Nasty Cherry.

Industry observers note that “I met [Charli XCX] on the set of a music video, and we ended up partying together for a few years,” she recalls. “I didn’t see her for a while, and then she reached out and was like, ‘I’m doing this project and I’ve been trying to cast the singer…’” Bechtel told Highsnobiety.

Unfortunately, Nasty Cherry is no longer active, with the group choosing to disband during the COVID-19 pandemic.

“We couldn’t do anything together, we couldn’t tour our second EP, and we weren’t able to make music together because we were all in different places in the world. So we just decided that it wasn’t going to work out anymore,” she revealed. “I miss it all the time. It ended too abruptly.”.

Bechtel also has a social media presence. Aside from her 1.6 million followers on Instagram, she has amassed 840,400 on TikTok, where she mostly posts cooking videos. In May 2023, she posted a video recreating Erewhon’s grain-free vegan blackout cake, which garnered 3 million views.

Per Highsnobiety, Bechtel shared that she got her love of cooking from her Mexican mother and Swiss-German father, both of whom would cook food from their respective cultures.

Industry observers note that “We ate dinner together as a family every single night, so there was always a fresh meal. We never had takeout,” she recalled. “We had a lot of Bon Appétit magazines lying around, so [my mother] would always try new recipes. I would come home and she’d have it open and be like, ‘I’m making this tonight,’ and she’d nail it. I would help her prep, so I grew up with my mom testing out stuff.”.

She also shared with Vogue that she is working on a cookbook and eventually would love to open up her own café.

“Not many people know this, but I’m really into interior design. So I’d love to open a space so people can have the full experience,” Bechtel stated.

Bechtel was born on July 28, 1997, making her a Leo. Healy, 37, was born on April 8, making him an Aries. According to the AstroTwins, per ELLE.com, “A pair of dynamic fire signs, Aries and Leo make a head-turning duo that whips up passion, adventure, and a heavy dose of drama everywhere you go. A flashy, outspoken pair, you’ll inspire envy. Get ready to reinvent the rules of relationships since your connection is certain to play by its own bold agenda.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For holiday dressing inspiration, look no further than Bianca Jagger and Sade for bold ensembles to re-create.
  • According to recent reports, winter is a season where artful layers and rich textures take center stage—notes these women knew how to hit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A little wardrobe inspiration is always welcome, especially when transitioning between seasons. As we move into winter, what better way to reinvigorate your wardrobe than by revisiting the style signifiers of some of fashion’s iconic muses? From Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and Lee Radziwill to Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy, their sartorial signatures remain as relevant today as ever.

For holiday dressing inspiration, look no further than Bianca Jagger and Sade for bold ensembles to re-create. For timeless winter layering tips, pay close attention to Ali McGraw and Iman; they shared a love for versatile neutrals (and knew when to rely on a statement belt for added punch). Off-duty ideas come courtesy of Princess Diana and Jane Birkin, who both had an affinity for dressing up more casual pieces.

According to recent reports, winter is a season where artful layers and rich textures take center stage—notes these women knew how to hit. Their enduring looks, which we’re breaking down for you below, are proof.

According to recent reports, jackie O knew the power of a statement coat. Here, she went for a knee-length animal-print style, with layered knits peeking out underneath for contrast. It’s a timeless yet modern look that’s easy enough to piece together; just pair it with a fitted pencil skirt and heeled ballerinas or loafers.

Sources indicate that for folklore flair, style a velvet duster coat with a turtleneck, corduroy trousers, and a statement belt. Flat leather boots and a slouchy beanie are the finishing touches.

According to recent reports, of course, Lee Radziwill was an early proponent of the pankou-closure jacket, which you’re probably seeing everywhere this season. Re-create her look for an 8 p.m. dinner res at Le Veau d’Or, with matching velvet trousers and elegant heeled mules.

In this enduring CBK look—one of the most recognizable style references—a simple black V-neck meets a cream-colored skirt, patent brown boots, and a no-fuss black leather handbag.

Chic yet comfy, this borrowed-from-the-boys look, inspired by Princess Di’s off-duty ’80s style, feels perfectly right for a lazy Sunday in the neighborhood.

A reason—or an excuse—to embrace winter whites. One of Jagger’s most iconic looks, this tonal ensemble is simple enough to put together. The key is to round out with accessories in complementary shades of cream and white.

Recent findings suggest that how Parisians dress for a rainy day. We love this mini-short-and-tights combo for milder winter weather.

According to recent reports, A layered fall look built around soft neutrals that can easily go from day to night. Lift a page from Iman’s style book by adding a hat to the mix, in whatever shape suits you best.

This outfit from Audrey Hepburn on set for Sabrina might be one of the chicest of all time. Make it yours with a matching cinched-waist blazer and skirt, topped off with a hat, kitten heels, and door-knocker earrings. Terrier not included!

Between the cuffs, leather gloves, and oversized belt, here’s proof that all black works best as a mix of textures.

Mexican artist Frida Kahlo loved a skirt; she was often photographed in a statement print or pattern. Re-create her look with a jacquard floral maxi paired with a velvet top, lace gloves, and silver earrings.

Everything Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams Have Mentioned About Their Friendship

📅 24 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • HBO Max and Crave’s Heated Rivalry has quickly become one of the most-discussed series of the year, catapulting its stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams into the celebrity stratosphere.
  • Storrie and Williams have been open in interviews about their experience creating the show, along with their offscreen relationship as they navigate sudden fame together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

HBO Max and Crave’s Heated Rivalry has quickly become one of the most-discussed series of the year, catapulting its stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams into the celebrity stratosphere. The two actors portray hockey players Shane Hollander (Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Storrie), who have a secret love affair spanning almost a decade. The series is known for its spicy intimate scenes as well as its beautiful depiction of romantic yearning.

Storrie and Williams have been open in interviews about their experience creating the show, along with their offscreen relationship as they navigate sudden fame together.

Sources indicate that “Hudson is my best friend, and I literally can’t fathom doing this without him,” Storrie told W magazine in December 2025. “We were both in similar places in life before this. We quit our jobs within a day of each other. We booked this and flew out the same day. Now it’s turning into two people who are being seen internationally for the first time. This has been the highlight of my life, and meeting Hudson makes that 10 times sweeter.”.

Here, everything the two actors have shared about their friendship.

According to recent reports, fans of the show tend to “ship” Williams and Storrie, hoping they end up dating in real life. Storrie addressed this head-on in an interview with Vulture, saying things are strictly platonic.

Recent findings suggest that when asked about the intimate scenes they shot in the show, Storrie noted, “For me, it doesn’t feel spicy at all—like, that’s me and my best friend. This is the first time in my life I’m having this many eyes on me. They’ve seen me naked, they’ve seen me kiss, they’ve seen me be in love with a man on-screen—it’s only normal for people to try to transfer that over to mine and Hudson’s real life.” He explained that he intends to keep his private life private, adding, “I feel honored to be able to bring someone to life that so many people feel seen, understood, and represented by, and I think that transcends whoever I’m sleeping with in my real life.”.

Williams expressed a similar sentiment to Deadline, saying, “I want queer people telling queer stories, but also, there’s the element of Connor and I—we’re best friends, and we love expressing that physically. You see people who infer or assume, and you kind of have to let that go. But then again, I never wanna stop expressing the love I have for Connor physically, and I’m never really going to, and I think multiple things can be true at once.”.

Sources indicate that in November 2026, Williams’s interview on The Assembly aired. One of the audience members there asked Williams if he ever had romantic feelings for Storrie. “No,” he replied. “Swiftly, me and Connor realized we were, like, platonic soulmates, just completely in love with each other. I think that’s what made our friendship so stable and beautiful, is that we realized we could be completely ourselves, be completely guard down. So, I think the thing that made our relationship as rich as it was is, like, me and that man could cuddle for 10 hours, and it just mean cuddling, just mean we just love each other dearly, but don’t wanna beep each other’s bop.”.

Recent findings suggest that he then added playfully, “Who doesn’t want Connor Storrie in their shower? You know, someone needs to get my back. I wish Connor was just with me every day. I’m like, ‘Hey, I have a loofah but I can’t reach [my back].’ If I had Connor with me every day, he could just come in there.”.

Sophie Nélisse, who plays Heated Rivalry’s Rose Landry, interviewed Williams for Wonderland magazine in January 2026 and asked him how he and Storrie balance promoting the show with forging their own identities. Williams admitted that they purposely go to different events, in part to keep their friendship more private and their brands separate.

“It’s been really nice, because Connor and I are aligned,” Williams began. “We want to be different artists. We don’t want to be the Olsen twins. We want to be Connor and Hudson, with different filmographies and different deals. As much as we love each other, our friendship doesn’t need to be public. Jacob [Tierney] has that quote: ‘Shane and Ilya are for the public. Connor and Hudson are for themselves.’ And that’s how we feel. People want to see us front row together all the time, but we actively avoid that, because it starts to feel like branding. If you’re always seen together, you become attached at the hip. I FaceTime him whenever I’m free. But if we’re offered the same fashion indicates, we’re like, ‘Which one are you going to? Okay, I’ll go to a different one.’ We’re stubborn, selfish artists who want to be our own people. We’re like, ‘I love you. I don’t want to do everything with you.’”.

Both Williams and Storrie got into great shape for the show. In a profile with GQ in December 2025, Williams talked about meeting his co-star and being intimidated by his build.

Recent findings suggest that “Connor pushed himself up onto the island in the kitchen,” Williams stated. “I remember seeing his arms. They were the size of my legs. I was like, Holy fuck.”.

Industry observers note that “It’s not true,” Storrie responded. “Because you have crazy legs.”.

In a recent development, the show’s creator, Jacob Tierney, also commented on their affection for one another in the piece, saying, “They’re living through a thing right now that is bananas—absolutely fucking bananas—and they’re handling it with grace, with humor, with generosity. They adore each other, which is like, thank fucking God.”.

While discussing his own workout routine with Men’s Health in January, Williams had a playful quip about Storrie’s physique: “I’m okay talking about my butt, but poor Connor Storrie—who has the fattest butt I’ve ever seen on a man—I’m sure just wants to stop talking about his beautiful cheeks.”.

In a December interview with Entertainment Weekly, the friends discussed a viral video from the Heated Rivalry wrap party where they are rolling around on the floor together.

“Very plainly spoken, me and Hudson are freaks,” Storrie explained. “We’re clowns. We just love to riff and have fun and go crazy, and those were two situations where we were caught off guard doing our thing. The wrap party, that was all improvised. I think we were just putting on a show.”.

Williams added, “Also, there might be something else, I think, with—we’re both very physical actors, and movement is a huge part of it.”.

During his Vulture interview, Storrie spoke about moving into an apartment next to Williams’s while filming in Toronto.

Van Cleef & Arpels Explores the Secrets and Mysteries of Ancient Egypt

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After archaeologist Howard Carter and his team discovered King Tutankhamun’s tomb in 1922, regal diadems, golden collars, and bold cuffs brought a fresh wave of Egyptian Revival into the Art Deco movement.
  • Recent findings suggest that from opulent collars to sculptural rings, each design harkens back to the arts, values, and beliefs that defined the Latest Kingdom.
  • It has been revealed that “There are a lot of real animals that were fashioned into amulets and small statues, likely to imbue the owners with some of their traits, but also to revere the creature and the benefits it provided,” archaeologist Randall Hixenbaugh tells Bazaar.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After archaeologist Howard Carter and his team discovered King Tutankhamun’s tomb in 1922, regal diadems, golden collars, and bold cuffs brought a fresh wave of Egyptian Revival into the Art Deco movement. Van Cleef & Arpels took note and added Egyptian-inspired calligraphy, hieroglyphs, and semiprecious stones into its lexicon of deco bracelets, sautoirs, and brooches, bringing a historic feel to the frostbitten glamour that defined the roaring ’20s. Now, over a century later, the maison’s new Fascinating Egypt high jewelry collection explores more avenues of the region’s mystical splendor.

Recent findings suggest that from opulent collars to sculptural rings, each design harkens back to the arts, values, and beliefs that defined the Latest Kingdom. But just as Egyptologists explored hidden messages beneath the grandeur of the 18th dynasty, Van Cleef conveys the mystique beneath its history. Shape-shifting necklaces function like secret passageways to new realms of expression, and Mysterioux brooches reincarnate sacred deities in gold and gemstones. Just take the Bennou, a terrestrial vessel for the sun god Ra, whose feathers of emeralds, marine-blue sapphires, lapis, cerulean slips of turquoise, mother of pearl, and drops of diamonds represent the colors of the earth. A blood-orange spessartite garnet with rays of diamonds hangs from a red spinel, like a drop of sunshine.

It has been revealed that “There are a lot of real animals that were fashioned into amulets and small statues, likely to imbue the owners with some of their traits, but also to revere the creature and the benefits it provided,” archaeologist Randall Hixenbaugh tells Bazaar. His namesake gallery in Manhattan’s Design District is home to artifacts sourced in accordance with the ethical standards set by the International Association of Dealers in Ancient Arts.

Sources indicate that talismans were worn like supplements to enhance the human experience—cats to spark joy, mongooses to offer protection from snakes, and frogs for fertility. Stones of certain colors were valued for their connotations with abundance and immortality. “The Egyptians prized bright blue and green materials, which were associated with the Nile, the sky, and life itself. Lapis lazuli was rare and valuable and therefore associated with the pharaohs. Its extensive use on King Tut’s gold mask highlights how highly regarded it was,” Hixenbaugh explains.

It has been revealed that the cobalt stone finds its way into all kinds of Van Cleef’s latest creations. It’s used generously in the “Ornement de Saphir” necklace, whose central totem resembles an evil eye, with an oval-cut sapphire pupil plopped cleverly in an iris of pavé diamonds. Suspended from a panel of lapis lazuli interspersed with slivers of gold and baguette-cut rubies, the pendant is detachable and can be worn like a brooch, while its Corde chain incorporates clasps concealed beneath colorful rondelles that allow it to transform into a pair of bracelets. A concept conceived in the 1940s, the versatile signature speaks to the ongoing conversation between the house’s heritage and Egypt’s mystique.

Some of Van Cleef’s most striking interpretations of the ancient kingdom come through in Art Deco bracelets. The articulated cuff style was a staple of the 1920s, with ample real estate for planes of illustrious motifs to flourish. Instead of a painter’s palette, Van Cleef brought diamonds, emeralds, and rubies together like dots on a pointillist painting through the “mystery set” technique (a manner of setting gemstones sans prongs).

According to recent reports, the house patented the method in the 1930s and has continued to enlist it to craft seamless gemscapes, extending into a series of “Paysage” bracelets. Clad in fields of gemstones, the deco-style pieces bring Egyptian royals, celestial skies, and monuments to life. Openwork, a technique that minimizes the use of solid metals, enables light to pass through each bejeweled mural, amplifying the high shine of each cuff. Other inconspicuous elements, like golden hieroglyphic nuggets, rest beneath articulated columns, like artifacts awaiting discovery.

The house’s bold fonts of design can be equally understood through the juxtaposition of lolly-like cabochons and sugar-white diamonds. Amid the sea of platinum and flashy Asscher cuts that defined Gatsby-era decadence, Van Cleef & Arpels brought teardrop emeralds into the mix. Suspended from pillars of diamonds set in platinum, the plump stones hung like enticing lozenges throughout a collaret necklace, circa 1929. The spellbinding masterpiece drew the eye of Egyptian royalty, Her Royal Highness Princess Faiza, who purchased the necklace in 1937. It was a convergence of brilliant facets and vivid, dome-shaped gems that bridged the gradual shift into midcentury modern shapes and matte stones. The provenance of the design influenced the maison’s updated rendition of the crown jewel, featuring luscious emeralds and slender pearls suspended from elongated pendants of white gold and diamonds.

Recent findings suggest that by the 1950s, Van Cleef’s interpretations of Egyptomania embraced organic forms, space-age ellipses, and plots of semiprecious stones. Smooth, matte surfaces of turquoise, malachite, and coral enhanced the realism of biomorphic designs, like a scarab clip with wings of turquoise, circa 1957. (The house would lend the brooch to the Petit Palais for the debut of “Tutankhamun and His Time” nearly a decade later.) Such vibrant stones extended into contemporary aesthetics of the 1980s, such as a collar necklace slathered in slices of jade, stripes of onyx, and birds carved out of coral.

This collection revisited the era through the language of Ettore Sottsass and the Memphis Group, a 1980s decorative arts firm, for spherical shapes and elements of cubism to take flight. Some of Sottsass’s most recognizable pieces include a sterling silver fruit stand with zigzag pillars and a colorblocked bookstand named “The Carlton.” Van Cleef translates this friction between elements smooth and sharp, glossy and matte into pieces like a saucer-shaped Mythe Celeste clip, coated in sheets of lapis and malachite with buttons of coral—elements beheld by the Egyptians as modalities of abundance and immortality. By contrast, a Frise Divine ring juxtaposes an oval-shaped Sri Lankan sapphire with a rigid tile of coral, and rows of diamonds set in zigzag streams of gold.

All creations in the Fascinating Egypt œuvre are united by tradition, a preservation of heritage echoed in the foundations of other art forms, like ballet. In fact, the house’s seamless dances of emeralds, rubies, and diamonds compelled George Balanchine to choreograph Jewels for the New York City Ballet in 1931—a moment that came full circle when the jewelers debuted a collection of ballerina clips and brooches a couple of years later. The nature of their anatomically sound arms, gilded in gold and ribbons of gemstones, extends into the collection’s Muse Éternelle brooches. Modeled after Cleopatra, the palm-sized figures are enrobed in a variety of dazzling threads of gold, strewn with diamonds, sapphires, rubies, and emeralds.
